text: Imagine the Sun, right now, replaced by a black hole with the same mass.
Would Earth get swallowed? No. Its pull out here would be the same, so we'd keep orbiting just like today.
The black hole itself would be tiny, about six kilometres wide, and it wouldn't even glow.
For about eight minutes, nothing changes. The last sunlight is still on its way.
Then the lights go out. The daytime sky turns black, and the Moon goes dark too.
In cities, street lights stay on all day, and solar panels stop making power.
Everyone turns the heating up at once, and power grids struggle to keep up.
Within a week, the average surface temperature drops to about minus eighteen degrees.
Plants stop making food. Crops die in the fields, and the animals that eat them go hungry.
The weather winds down too. Without the Sun's heat, there's little left to drive the wind and rain.
Within a year, about minus seventy. The oceans freeze over, and the ice keeps getting thicker.
A few people might hang on underground, using nuclear and geothermal power. Deep below the ice, life at hot vents keeps going.
The good news: this can't happen. The Sun is far too small to ever become a black hole.
So the real nightmare isn't being swallowed. It's orbiting perfectly around something that no longer keeps us alive.
